# 1 Reproducible report and data description

## 1.1 Introduction

The watershed dataset is a synthetic dataset relating `snowpack_pct_normal`, `precip_mm`, and `mean_temp_c` to `streamflow_index`. This document aims to fit and diagnose a linear model using these predictors to model the response, `streamflow_index` using matrix computation in python.

## 1.2 Data Inspection and Validation

```{python}
# Libraries
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

```{python}
# Load CSV
df = pd.read_csv("data/raw/watershed.csv")
```


Data Inspection
```{python}
print(f"Data Frame first 5 rows: \n{df.head()} \n\n")
print(f"Shape: {df.shape} \n \n")
print(f"Data types: \n{df.dtypes} \n \n")
print(f"Missingness: \n{df.isna().sum()} \n \n")
print(f"Are IDs Unique? {df["id"].is_unique} \n \n")
```

The Watershed dataset contains 125 observations with 5 fields: `id`, `snowpack_pct_normal`, `precip_mm`, `mean_temp_c`, and `streamflow_index`. All variables have a `float64` data type except for `id`, which has a type of `int64`. There is no missingness coded as `None` or `NA` in any field and IDs are unique. At this point, there are no data quality concerns.

# 2 Matrix setup and standardization
```{python}
predictors = df[[
    "snowpack_pct_normal",
    "precip_mm",
    "mean_temp_c"]].to_numpy()

y = df["streamflow_index"].to_numpy()
```

## 2.1 Predictor standardization

```{python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (
predictors - means
) / sds
```

Verify approximately:
```{python}
print(f"Means (snowpack_pct_normal, precip_mm, mean_temp_c): \n{Z.mean(axis=0)} \n")
print(f"Standard Deviations (snowpack_pct_normal, precip_mm mean_temp_c): \n{Z.std(axis=0)} \n")
```

The standardization normalizes each value in each predictor column such that their distributions resemble that of a normal distribution $\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. The means of each predictor column are approximately zero, and the standard deviations are 1, showing a successful normaliztion.

## 2.2 Construct the design matrix

```{python}
# Add an intercept column:
X = np.column_stack([
np.ones(len(Z)),
Z ])
```

```{python}
print(f"Shape of predictors: {predictors.shape}\n")
print(f"shape of Z: {Z.shape}\n")
print(f"shape of X: {X.shape}\n")
print(f"shape of y: {y.shape}\n")
print(f"matrix rank of X: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)}\n")
# -1 removes the 1s column (intercept) from the rank of the design matrix, counting only predictors
print(f"number of predictors excluding the intercept: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)-1}\n")
```

X and y must have compatible shapes because one row of parameters in X represents one observation, corresponding to one response in each row of y. The intercept column is included as all 1s to apply an equal $\beta_0$ parameter to each value and to represent the baseline value when all predictor values are zero. This dataset has values in `precip_mm` that are generally 20 times higher than those of `mean_temp_c`. Standardizing the predictors places all their values on a common scale of deviation from the mean, so they have similarly scaled parameters and the regression is more consistant. Numpy broadcasting allows operations on arrays of compatible shapes and performs these operations element-by-element by vectorizing the equation.

# 3 Least Squares

## 3.1 Fit a linear model
```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X,y,rcond=None)
print(f"Estimated Coefficients: {beta_hat}")
print(f"Intercept: {round(beta_hat[0], 3)}")
print(f"normalized snowpack_pct_normal: {round(beta_hat[1], 3)}")
print(f"normalized precip_mm: {round(beta_hat[2], 3)}")
print(f"normalized mean_temp_c: {round(beta_hat[3], 3)}")
```

The predictor with the largest absolute value coefficient is the intercept $\beta_0$.

## 3.2 Calculate fitted values and residuals
```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted
```

```{python}
rmse = np.sqrt(
np.mean(
residuals ** 2))
print(f"Residuals mean: {residuals.mean()}\n")
print(f"RMSE: {round(rmse, 4)}")
```

`X @ beta_hat` is the matrix multiplication $X\hat{\vec{\beta}}$ which results in the vector of predicted values $\hat{\vec{y}}$ created using the linear model. The residual mean is nearly zero, indicating the model is finding the best fit line between all given predictor values such that their distances from the line ($(y_i -\hat(y_i))^2$) cancel each other out: the model does not over or under predict any particular values. RMSE summarizes the typical distance of a residual point from the mean zero, or the average magnitude of error. This value matches the standard deviation of residuals. In these calculations, we use `X @ beta_hat` instead of `X * beta_hat` because the former is standard matrix multiplication and the latter is an element-wise matrix multiplication that applies `beta_hat` down each column and does not sum any values.

# 4 QR, SVD, and conditioning

## 4.1 QR decomposition
```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
print(f"Shape Q: {Q.shape}\n")
print(f"Shape R: {R.shape}\n")
```

```{python}
#Verify Q@R = X:
print(f"Q @ R equals X, within tolarance: {np.allclose( # both matricies are approximately equal element-wise 
Q @ R,
X)}\n")
```

```{python}
print(f"Q transposed @ Q equals the identity matrix I, within tolarance: {np.allclose(
Q.T @ Q,
np.eye(Q.shape[1])
)}\n")
```

## 4.2 SVD
```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(
X, full_matrices=False)

print(f"Shape of U: {U.shape}\n")
print(f"Shape of s: {s.shape}\n")
print(f"Shape of Vt: {Vt.shape}\n")

print(f"Singular Values: {s}\n")
```

Reconstruct X ($U \dot s \dot Vt$):
```{python}
X_reconstructed = (
U@ np.diag(s)
@ Vt)
```

```{python}
# Verify:
print(f"SVD Reconstruction of X is equal to X, within tolerance: {np.allclose(
X_reconstructed,
X)}")
```

## 4.3 Rank and conditioning

```{python}
print(f"Rank of X: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)} \n")
print(f"Condition value of normalized X: {round(np.linalg.cond(X), 3)} \n")
```

Raw, unstandardized design matrix:
```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([
np.ones(len(predictors)),
predictors
])
```
and report:
```{python}
raw_cond = np.linalg.cond(X_raw)
print(f"Condition value of raw X matrix: {round(raw_cond, 3)}")
```

Q @ R $\approx$ X verifies that Q and R are the factored decomposition of X into orthogonal and upper triangular matricies, Q and R. Q.T @ Q $\approx$ I verifies Q is indeed orthogonal. The singular values $\sigma$ of the SVD show the directions in which the linear model is most and least drawn towards and therefore most and least represented in the model.

A large condition number suggests the predictors are sensitive to small changes and that the predictors are nearly linearly dependent. After standardization, the condition number decreased from ```{python}round(raw_cond, 3)``` to ```{python}round(np.linalg.cond(X), 3)```. This suggests the standardization of predictors reduces their sensitivity to small pertubations. The measurment scale of a predictor can affect the raw condition number because their raw values are measured in units may be are orders of magnitude different. The low condition number indicates the standardized design matrix does not show evidence of severe near-redundancy among predictors.

# 5 Reproducibility and numerical computing reflection

Clean execution in computational reports matters because it allows for the results to be reproducable by anyone with access to the code base. It also helps give evidence for each finding and supports results by employing literate programming to show the narrative alongside supporting code and results. Reusable code should not depend on hidden notebook state because it may appear correct, but an unintuitive or undisclosed order of cell execution will cause the results to not be reproducable or for data to be inadvertantly overwritten. It is preferrable to use `np.linalg.lstsq()` over manually computing $(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$ in ordinary numerical work because the manual computation includes rounding after each step when done on a computer. A solution using `np.linalg.lstsq()` will be more precise. This appoximation in computer-based solutions with floating point math is also why checks for QR and SVD reconstruction prefer `np.allclose()`.
